content.title: About
content.content: Meringue cookie is a light, crisp treat made from egg whites, sugar, and a touch of starch. The mixture is whipped into a stiff foam and baked at low temperature, giving the biscuit its characteristic airy, melt‑in‑the‑mouth texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meringue originated in France in the 17th century and was first used as a decorative element for desserts.
Sugar not only sweetens the meringue but also stabilizes the protein foam, allowing it to hold its shape during baking.
The cookies can be flavored with vanilla, lemon zest, cocoa powder, or spices.
Thin meringue sheets are often used in pastry cakes as a “crystalline” layer.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Because most of the mass is egg white and sugar, meringue cookies contain far less fat than typical baked goods.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Egg whites provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Meringue is naturally free of gluten, making it suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Since the main ingredient is egg white, meringue can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with egg allergies.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The large amount of sugar gives meringue a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to tooth decay and weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Meringue cookies can be enjoyed on their own, used as a base for layered cakes, as a garnish for ice cream, incorporated into chocolate fondues, or broken into pieces and topped with fresh berries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store meringue cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption, which makes them soft.
